reply.text: `==` tests whether two objects have equal values, calling `__eq__` under the hood. `is` tests whether two names refer to the exact same object in memory, comparing identity (roughly, `id(a) == id(b)`). Two equal values can be distinct objects, so `[1, 2] == [1, 2]` is `True` but `[1, 2] is [1, 2]` is `False`. Use `is` for singletons like `None` (`x is None`), and `==` for value comparison. Avoid using `is` to compare numbers or strings by value: CPython caches some small ints and interned strings, so results can look right by accident and then break.
